# Field Office WAN Transformation and Distribution Point Consolidation {.unnumbered}

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**[Download this whitepaper as DOCX](field-office-wan-transformation-dp-consolidation.docx)** — a Word copy of
this page, regenerated on every site deploy. (Also available from the
**Other Formats** link in the page sidebar.)
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Read this first

Every cost figure in this paper is an indicative planning estimate derived
from published list pricing and industry benchmarks. None is a quote.

The financial case rests on one number this paper does not yet hold:
current MPLS cost per field office per month. Section 9 identifies this
and eight other assumptions that must be validated before any figure here
is used in a budget submission.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## In this whitepaper

A proposal is under consideration to invest approximately \$50,000,000
refreshing Configuration Manager distribution point hardware at roughly
1,500 field offices. This paper argues the investment addresses a symptom
rather than a cause, targets a tier the agency has already decided to
retire, and can be replaced by a network modernization program that costs
less, delivers more, and is a prerequisite for the Microsoft Intune
migration already underway.

This paper shares its transport argument with
[SD-WAN vs. DIA Under TIC 3.0](tic3-sdwan-vs-dia.qmd) and its INR/GCC
finding with [Next Generation DNS](infoblox-hybrid-dns-unified-ddi.qmd);
both are cited rather than re-derived. Its own contribution is the
distribution-point unit-economics argument in Sections 2–3, the
distribution-point-vs.-Intune compliance comparison in Section 3.4
(detailed in Appendix A.1), the gated (not calendar-based) all-in
cutover trigger in Section 4.7, and the compliance/reporting case for
SD-WAN and TIC 3.0 that holds independent of the cost model, in
Section 4.8 (detailed in Appendix A.2) — none of which are covered
elsewhere in this corpus.
:::

## Executive Summary

The proposal, its rationale, and this paper's counter-argument are
summarized in the box above. The five findings below are that
argument's evidentiary basis — the unit economics, the capacity math,
and the cost model that Sections 2 through 6 develop in full.

### Findings

- **The unit economics do not support the estimate.** \$50M across 1,500
  sites is \$33,333 per office, against \$3,500 to \$12,000 for a
  correctly specified distribution point. The figure is either a
  five-year total cost of ownership presented as an equipment refresh,
  or it bundles scope that is not a distribution point.

- **Capacity requires 24 distribution points, not 1,500.** Microsoft
  documents a ceiling of 4,000 clients per distribution point.[^dp-limits]
  At an estimated 70,000 endpoints, capacity is satisfied by 24
  distribution points across 12 hub sites — a 98.4% reduction.

- **The remaining 1,476 exist to work around constrained branch
  circuits.** Distribution point count at this scale is driven entirely
  by network topology, never by Configuration Manager capacity. The
  correct response is to fix the network.

- **Network modernization is cheaper and may be cash-positive.** An
  SD-WAN overlay with dedicated internet access and 5G secondary paths
  at all 1,500 offices requires roughly \$10.0M in first-year capital
  and \$15.7M recurring. Above \$873 per site per month of current MPLS
  spend, the program funds itself.

- **The same 12 hub sites serve three programs.** SD-WAN aggregation,
  regional internet breakout, and the consolidated content tier
  co-locate at one set of facilities under one accreditation boundary
  — and become the Microsoft Connected Cache footprint as co-management
  matures.

[^dp-limits]: [Size and scale — Configuration Manager (Microsoft Learn)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/intune/configmgr/core/plan-design/configs/size-and-scale-numbers). Every capacity figure in Section 3.1 is sourced from this page.

### Headline comparison

| Option | Yr 1 capital | 5-yr net | What it delivers |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Distribution point refresh (proposed)** | \$50.0M | −\$50.0M | Content delivery only; capital into a retiring tier |
| **SD-WAN + DIA + 5G, DP consolidation** | \$10.0M | +\$7.7M\* | Content, M365, Teams, video, Intune enablement, TIC 3.0 breakout |
| **Do nothing** | \$0 | \$0 | Aging DPs, constrained branches, Intune migration blocked |

*Five-year positions assume phased migration with savings ramping from
year 2. \*The network program's 5-yr net additionally depends on
Assumption 1 (current MPLS cost per site — not yet validated; see
Section 9); it is a base-case figure, not a floor. Section 6 gives the
model and sensitivity analysis.*

::: {.callout-tip}
## Recommendation

Defer the \$50M distribution point refresh pending completion of a
network modernization assessment.

Fund a Phase 0 design and pilot (approximately \$1.8M, six months)
covering architecture, the TIC 3.0 Branch Office accreditation package,
and a ten-site pilot spanning all transport types.

Validate the nine assumptions in Section 9 — beginning with current
MPLS cost per site, which determines whether this program is
cash-positive or net-new cost.
:::

## 1. Purpose and Scope

This paper evaluates a proposed capital investment in Configuration
Manager distribution point hardware at field offices and presents an
alternative architecture. It addresses three questions:

1. Is a distribution point required at every field office?
2. If not, how many are required, and where should they be placed?
3. What network investment is required to make a consolidated content
   tier viable, and how does its cost compare?

### 1.1 In scope

- Configuration Manager content distribution architecture for
  approximately 1,500 field offices
- Branch wide-area network transport, edge platform, and secondary path
  design
- Hub site count, placement rationale, and content tier sizing
- Comparative five-year cost model with sensitivity analysis
- Transition alignment with the Microsoft Intune migration and
  co-management program

### 1.2 Out of scope

- Air-gapped and separately accredited enclaves. These retain
  Configuration Manager and local distribution points indefinitely and
  are unaffected by anything in this paper.
- Data center and headquarters campus network design
- Endpoint hardware refresh, application packaging, and Intune workload
  migration sequencing
- Voice, contact center, and physical security network requirements

### 1.3 Cloud environment constraint

All cloud-dependent elements are scoped exclusively to Microsoft 365
Government Community Cloud (GCC), aligned to FedRAMP Moderate. No
element of this design depends on GCC High, Department of Defense, or
commercial cloud tenancy. This constraint is favorable for most Intune
capability: documented Microsoft Intune feature gaps concentrate in GCC
High and DoD environments, while GCC feature availability tracks
substantially closer to commercial.

One named exception applies, and it is addressed directly rather than
left open: Microsoft 365 Informed Network Routing does not extend to
this environment. Section 4.6 states the finding and its source.

## 2. The Proposal Under Review

The proposal requests approximately \$50,000,000 to refresh
Configuration Manager distribution point hardware across the field
office estate. Divided across 1,500 offices, this is \$33,333 per site.

### 2.1 Unit cost reconciliation

| Configuration | Unit cost | × 1,500 | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Micro form factor PC, right-sized** | \$3,500 | \$5.3M | Adequate for a small branch; no ECC or out-of-band management |
| **1U rack server, ECC, iDRAC, redundant PSU** | \$12,000 | \$18.0M | Appropriate server-class platform |
| **1U server plus \$4,000 per-site deployment** | \$16,000 | \$24.0M | Includes field installation labor |
| **Proposed estimate** | **\$33,333** | **\$50.0M** | **Approximately 2x the fully loaded server case** |

The gap indicates one of two things, and the distinction is material to
any comparison:

- **A five-year total cost of ownership presented as an equipment
  refresh.** Plausible: hardware, warranty extension, deployment labor
  across 1,500 dispersed sites, compliance sustainment, and contractor
  overhead reach this figure. If so, the alternative must be compared on
  a total cost of ownership basis, which Section 6 provides.
- **Bundled scope beyond the distribution point.** Circuit upgrades,
  branch switching, uninterruptible power, or racks. All legitimate to
  fund; none of them is a distribution point, and each should be
  evaluated on its own merits.

::: {.callout-note}
## Decomposition request

Before any comparison is credible, the sponsoring organization should
state whether the \$50M figure is acquisition cost or five-year total
cost of ownership, and itemize any scope beyond the distribution point
itself.
:::

### 2.2 The timing problem

Independent of unit cost, the investment is directed at an
infrastructure tier the agency has already decided to reduce. The
endpoint management strategy is a migration to Microsoft Intune, and
Microsoft has been explicit about the platform direction: Intune
receives all new device management innovation, while Configuration
Manager continues to serve on-premises devices with a focus on security,
stability, and long-term support. Configuration Manager moves to an
annual release cadence beginning with version 2609 in September 2026.

Configuration Manager is not end-of-life, and the distribution point
role is not deprecated. But hardware purchased in FY26 depreciates
through FY31. If the co-management program completes within three to
four years, the agency will have funded 1,500 devices for one to two
years beyond their usefulness and will own the disposal cost.

This is also a doctrine question, not only a depreciation question.
UIAO's Intune-First Asset Onboarding doctrine (ADR-071) prohibits
net-new SCCM co-management deployments for new endpoints — existing
co-management workloads continue under their migration path, but new
workloads must enter Intune-first. The 24-distribution-point content
tier proposed in Section 4 is sized to consolidate the *existing*
1,500-site footprint, not to expand it; any budget submission built on
this paper should state that framing explicitly so it reads as
compliant with, rather than in tension with, that doctrine.

::: {.callout-note}
## The question that sizes the requirement

What is the planned distribution point count at the completion of the
co-management program, and in what fiscal year?

If this cannot be answered, the refresh cannot be sized — a refresh
requires a target inventory. If the answer is a number materially
below 1,500, the proposal is buying assets with a useful life shorter
than their depreciation schedule.
:::

## 3. Why Per-Office Distribution Points Are No Longer the Right Model

The distribution point is a content host. Configuration Manager
separates policy from content: the management point issues instructions,
and the distribution point serves the bytes. The role has no database,
no policy engine, and no client relationship — it is Internet
Information Services delivering hash-named files from a single-instance
content library over BITS, with an agent for content management. That
thinness is why the placement question is an economics question rather
than a functional one.

### 3.1 Published capacity limits

All figures in this table are sourced from Microsoft's Configuration
Manager size-and-scale documentation.[^dp-limits]

| Constraint | Documented limit | Implication at this scale |
|---|---|---|
| **Clients per distribution point** | 4,000 | 70,000 endpoints require 18 at ceiling; 24 with headroom |
| **Standard distribution points per site** | 250 | A 1,500-DP topology is impossible without pull DPs |
| **Pull distribution points per site (additional)** | 2,000 | 1,500 is feasible only as 250 standard plus 1,250 pull |
| **Total DPs per primary site** | 5,000 | Hierarchy-wide ceiling — the primary site's own DPs plus all DPs belonging to its child secondary sites. This design uses a stand-alone primary site with no secondary sites, so the binding ceiling is the 2,250 figure above (250 standard + 2,000 pull), not this row |
| **Clients per stand-alone primary site** | 150,000 Windows | 70,000 endpoints fit comfortably in one site |
| **Packages and applications per DP** | 10,000 | Not a binding constraint |

**The decisive figure is the first row.** On capacity grounds, 70,000
endpoints require 24 distribution points. The proposal contemplates
1,500. The additional 1,476 exist solely to compensate for constrained
branch transport — they serve no Configuration Manager requirement
whatsoever.

### 3.2 The cost of the distributed model

| Dimension | At 1,500 distribution points |
|---|---|
| **Duplicated storage** | 1.5 to 3 petabytes of replicated content, most never requested at most sites |
| **Distribution fan-out** | Every package replicates to 1,500 targets; Microsoft warns that pull DPs request content simultaneously and may request all available content, loading source DPs and delaying distribution |
| **Topology complexity** | Requires tiered pull hierarchy, distribution point groups, and staggered scheduling to remain stable |
| **Compliance sustainment** | 1,500 accredited systems to baseline, scan, patch, and carry in the system security plan |
| **Field support** | No out-of-band management on micro form factor platforms; every hang is a site visit |
| **Refresh obligation** | A recurring capital event every five years, indefinitely |

### 3.3 What has changed since the model was adopted

- **Content has moved to the cloud.** Windows Update, Microsoft 365
  Apps, Defender definitions, Store applications, and Intune Win32
  applications originate from Microsoft content delivery networks, not
  from an on-premises content library. Delivery Optimization and
  Microsoft Connected Cache address this class of traffic without
  agency-owned content infrastructure.
- **Peer distribution matured.** Peer Cache and BranchCache allow
  designated clients at a site to serve content to peers over the local
  network, requiring one wide-area transfer per site rather than one per
  client — with no server, no accreditation, and no refresh cycle.
- **Branch transport economics inverted.** The per-office distribution
  point model was justified against expensive, congested, low-bandwidth
  branch circuits. Commercial broadband and dedicated internet access at
  200 Mbps to 1 Gbps now cost a fraction of legacy MPLS at a fraction of
  the bandwidth.

::: {.callout-important}
## The accurate statement

The distribution point role is not obsolete. The
distribution-point-per-office topology is.

Distribution points remain the correct mechanism for serving
Configuration Manager content to on-premises clients. What is obsolete
is the assumption that every branch requires a local copy of the
content library.
:::

### 3.4 Distribution points vs. Intune — a compliance comparison

Independent of the economics and capacity math in Sections 3.1–3.3, a
distribution point and Intune sit in structurally different compliance
postures — different SSP footprint, different hardening responsibility,
different continuous-evidence posture, control by control. That
comparison is detailed in Appendix A.1 rather than here, to keep this
section on the cost and capacity argument. The finding that carries
forward into the cost model: for as long as any distribution point
exists — 1,500 today, 24 under this design's Section 4 target, or
whatever smaller number Section 4.7's gates eventually allow — its
compliance sustainment is a program in addition to, not instead of,
whatever already covers the Intune-managed fleet. Section 3.2's
"compliance sustainment" line item is this program, understated:
consolidating to 24 distribution points shrinks it to roughly a
twelfth of its former size, but it does not shrink to zero, and it
does not shrink at all until Section 4.7's gates close.

## 4. Proposed Target Architecture

### 4.1 Design principles

1. Size the content tier to client capacity, not to office count.
2. Solve the transport problem at the transport layer rather than
   working around it with distributed content.
3. Co-locate network aggregation, internet breakout, and content
   services at one set of hub facilities under one accreditation
   boundary.
4. Design the hub tier so it becomes the Microsoft Connected Cache
   footprint without re-siting or re-accrediting.
5. Sequence branch migration to contract renewal dates so the program
   funds itself progressively.
6. Treat every cloud-dependent optimization as an enhancement, never as
   a design dependency.

### 4.2 Hub topology — 12 sites

Twelve hub sites are proposed, aligned to existing agency geography so
that no new real estate, power, or accreditation boundary is required.

| Hub class | Count | Location basis | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary data center** | 1 | Headquarters campus | Source content library, SD-WAN control plane primary, breakout |
| **Secondary data center** | 1 | Existing disaster recovery facility | Source library replica, control plane secondary, breakout |
| **Regional hub** | 10 | Existing regional office locations | SD-WAN aggregation, regional internet breakout, pull distribution points |

Twelve sites places every branch within a defensible latency envelope of
an aggregation point and, critically, produces a security perimeter that
can realistically be monitored and accredited. Local internet breakout
at 1,500 sites is a multi-year zero-trust undertaking. Breakout at 12
sites is achievable within a single accreditation package, which is why
regional breakout is the standard federal stepping stone. This is the
same physics-and-accreditation argument made in
[SD-WAN vs. DIA Under TIC 3.0](tic3-sdwan-vs-dia.qmd); this paper does
not re-derive it.

### 4.3 Content tier — 24 distribution points

Distribution point count is derived from managed endpoint population
against the documented 4,000-client ceiling, with headroom for growth
and for regional imbalance.

| Sizing input | Value | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| **Managed endpoints (estimate)** | 70,000 | To be validated — see Section 9 |
| **Supported clients per distribution point** | 4,000 | Microsoft published limit[^dp-limits] |
| **Theoretical minimum distribution points** | 18 | 70,000 divided by 4,000 |
| **Design target utilization** | 73% | Headroom for growth and regional imbalance |
| **Distribution points deployed** | **24** | **2 per hub site across 12 sites** |
| **Deployed capacity** | **96,000 clients** | **37% headroom over current estimate** |

**Distribution point allocation**

| Site | DPs | Type | Function |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary data center** | 2 | Standard (source) | Full content library; source for all pull DPs; HA pair |
| **Secondary data center** | 2 | Standard (source) | Full library replica; secondary pull source; HA pair |
| **Regional hubs (10 sites)** | 20 | Pull | Targeted content subset; 2 per site for capacity and availability |
| **Total** | **24** | — | **96,000 client capacity across 12 sites** |

Configuring regional hubs as pull distribution points sourcing from the
two data centers removes distribution load from the site server and
confines the fan-out problem to a 2-to-20 relationship rather than
1-to-1,500. Content targeting via distribution point groups further
limits each regional hub to the packages its region actually consumes.

**Storage sizing per distribution point**

| Tier | Usable storage | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Data center source DP** | 8 TB | Full content library plus growth and prestaging staging area |
| **Regional pull DP** | 4 TB | Targeted subset, estimated at 60% of full library, plus growth |
| **Assumed current library size** | 1.5 TB | To be validated by measuring SCCMContentLib on an existing DP |

::: {.callout-note}
## Sizing trigger

Add two distribution points per 8,000 net new managed endpoints, or
when sustained utilization at any hub exceeds 3,200 clients per
distribution point (80% of the supported ceiling).

If the validated endpoint population exceeds 90,000, increase to 28
distribution points by adding a third DP at the four largest regional
hubs.
:::

### 4.4 Branch network

Every field office receives a dual-path design: a primary dedicated
internet access circuit sized to seat count, and a 5G fixed wireless
secondary path for continuity. An SD-WAN overlay provides application-
aware routing and segmentation; this paper illustrates the bill of
materials with one vendor's product line (Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN) as a
worked example, not as an exclusive recommendation — the underlying
sizing and topology argument is vendor-neutral, and UIAO's own
[SD-WAN modernization spec](../modernization-specs/sdwan/sdwan.qmd) and
[OrgPath composability matrix](orgpath-composability-matrix.qmd) treat
SD-WAN as an adapter class rather than a single-vendor commitment.

| Tier | Sites | Seats | Primary circuit | Edge platform |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **S** | 750 | Up to 25 | 200–300 Mbps DIA | Catalyst C8200L-1N-4T |
| **M** | 525 | 26–50 | 500 Mbps DIA | Catalyst C8200-1N-4T |
| **L** | 225 | 51–100 | 1 Gbps DIA | Catalyst C8300-1N1S-4T2X |
| **All** | 1,500 | — | 5G secondary path | P-5GS6-GL module or CG522-E gateway |

- **Symmetric and SLA-backed beats raw bandwidth.** A 20-seat office
  does not need a gigabit. It needs low jitter and a service level
  agreement. 300 Mbps of dedicated internet access outperforms 1 Gbps of
  best-effort cable for voice, virtual desktop, and Teams.
- **5G is a continuity path, not a capacity path.** Carrier fixed
  wireless is subject to deprioritization and data policy. It will keep
  an office transacting through an outage. It will not carry a feature
  update wave, and content deployment policy should exclude the
  secondary path.
- **Verify diversity physically.** Cable plus 5G is genuinely diverse.
  Two nominally different fiber providers frequently share the same
  conduit into the building. Require documented physical path diversity
  per site.
- **Confirm crypto throughput licensing.** Encrypted throughput on this
  class of edge platform is typically license-tiered. Purchasing 1 Gbps
  circuits against a 250 Mbps crypto tier is the most common and most
  expensive costing error on this platform.

### 4.5 Security and TIC 3.0

Regional internet breakout requires the agency to operate under a CISA
Trusted Internet Connections 3.0 Branch Office use case, with a
cloud-delivered security stack replacing the inspection previously
performed at the centralized gateway. The full argument for why TIC 3.0
governs this decision — and why transport and governance are separate
questions — is made in
[SD-WAN vs. DIA Under TIC 3.0](tic3-sdwan-vs-dia.qmd); this section
states only the consequence for this program.

This is the program critical path. Circuits can be ordered in ninety
days. An authorized local-breakout security architecture cannot.
Beginning at twelve hub sites rather than 1,500 branches reduces the
accreditation surface by two orders of magnitude and is the primary
reason the phased approach in Section 7 starts at the hubs.

### 4.6 Microsoft 365 optimization — Informed Network Routing

Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Cloud OnRamp for SaaS integrates with Microsoft
365 Informed Network Routing (INR) for WW Commercial tenants. Microsoft
Learn states this integration explicitly and lists Cisco Catalyst
SD-WAN as the only SD-WAN vendor in the "Currently enabled solutions"
table for INR.

::: {.callout-important}
## INR is not available to this program's cloud environment — closed, not open

Section 1.3 scopes this program to Microsoft 365 GCC, aligned to FedRAMP
Moderate. Microsoft Learn (updated 2026-03-10) states verbatim that
*"Microsoft 365 informed network routing supports tenants in WW
Commercial cloud but not the GCC Moderate, GCC High, DoD, Germany, or
China clouds."* This is not an item pending confirmation — it is a
documented exclusion that applies directly to this program's scope, and
is analyzed in full, with a machine-enforced contract fixture encoding
the exclusion, in
[Next Generation DNS](infoblox-hybrid-dns-unified-ddi.qmd), Part 9, and
in Vol I Book 05, Appendix A of the Federal Organization Compliance
series.

The absence of INR does not eliminate SD-WAN's value for this program.
Direct internet breakout with DSCP marking and application-aware
routing using locally observed path metrics (rather than Microsoft-
supplied telemetry) remain fully available in GCC and are the pattern
this program should plan around from the outset — not as a Phase 3
enhancement pending vendor confirmation, but as the baseline design.
:::

Phase 3 in Section 7 is revised accordingly: it no longer treats INR
as an enhancement to enable "subject to accreditation," since the
telemetry channel required for INR to function is not offered to this
cloud environment at all.

### 4.7 The all-in trigger — when to retire the last distribution point

Section 4.3 sizes a 24-distribution-point tier as the *interim*
consolidated state, not a new permanent floor. Configuration Manager's
own co-management model exposes seven workload sliders — Compliance
policies, Windows Update policies, Endpoint Protection, Device
configuration, Office Click-to-Run apps, and Client apps (Resource
access policies was deprecated in version 2203)[^comanage-workloads] —
and a distribution point still has work to do for every workload that
has not switched to Intune. "Some workloads are on Intune" is not the
same claim as "the content tier can be decommissioned," and the two get
conflated in most modernization timelines. This section states the
difference as a checklist rather than a date.

**Retire the last distribution point only when all five gates below are
closed — not on a calendar milestone:**

| Gate | Closed when | Why it's binding |
|---|---|---|
| **1. App content** | Client Apps and Office Click-to-Run Apps workloads are switched to Intune for the full validated endpoint population | Until switched, apps deployed from Configuration Manager remain in Software Center and still pull from a distribution point; only content already migrated to Intune's Company Portal path stops needing one[^comanage-workloads] |
| **2. Update content** | Windows Update Policies and Device Configuration workloads are switched to Intune | Same mechanism as Gate 1, applied to feature/quality updates rather than apps; this pairing is also Microsoft's own prerequisite for Windows Autopatch, a useful external forcing function to anchor the timeline to[^autopatch-prereq] |
| **3. OS provisioning** | Bare-metal imaging has moved from Configuration Manager task sequences to Windows Autopilot (user-driven, pre-provisioned, or device preparation) | OS deployment is not a co-management workload at all — it is the one dependency the slider model doesn't cover, and the most common reason a "just in case" distribution point survives after every workload above has switched |
| **4. Content caching role** | Any Microsoft Connected Cache instance has moved off distribution-point hardware, or is not needed given the DIA circuits this program installs | Microsoft Connected Cache can run *on* a Configuration Manager distribution point and continue serving Intune Win32 app content to co-managed clients — meaning a distribution point can survive the first three gates in a caching-only role and still require patching, accreditation, and a site-system footprint[^mcc-win32] |
| **5. Compliance evidence** | Compliance policy and Endpoint Protection reporting no longer cite the Configuration Manager site database as their evidence source | Closing content delivery does not by itself close the compliance-reporting dependency; confirm with the security architecture organization before decommissioning the site infrastructure that produces this evidence |

::: {.callout-note}
## This is a gate, not a date

Phase 3 in Section 7 treats Configuration Manager scope as narrowing "in
line with co-management progress." That phrasing is intentionally
non-committal because the honest trigger is the five gates above, not a
fixed month. An agency that reaches all five gates in month 30 should
retire its last distribution point in month 30, not wait for a Phase 3
date chosen before co-management maturity (Assumption 7, Section 9) was
known. An agency that has not reached them by month 60 should keep the
24-distribution-point tier rather than force a cutover against an open
gate.
:::

[^comanage-workloads]: [Co-management workloads (Microsoft Learn)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/intune/configmgr/comanage/workloads).
[^autopatch-prereq]: [Prerequisites for Windows Autopatch (Microsoft Learn)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/deployment/windows-autopatch/prepare/windows-autopatch-prerequisites) — requires the Windows Update Policies and Device Configuration workloads to be managed by Intune.
[^mcc-win32]: [Microsoft Connected Cache with Configuration Manager — support for Intune Win32 apps (Microsoft Learn)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/intune/configmgr/core/plan-design/hierarchy/microsoft-connected-cache#support-for-intune-win32-apps).

### 4.8 Compliance and reporting drivers, independent of cost

Sections 2 through 6 make the economic case: even under downside MPLS
assumptions, this program is cheaper than the proposed refresh. That
economic case is not the only one — NIST, CISA, and the OrgComp
control-closure ledger this corpus maintains give the agency reasons to
build SD-WAN and TIC 3.0 branch breakout at these 1,500 sites that hold
even if Section 6.3's sensitivity analysis had come out unfavorably.
The control-by-control mapping (SC-7, SC-8, AC-4, SI-3, SI-4, AU-12,
CP-8), the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model v2.0 cross-cutting-capability
argument, and the BOD-25-01 sequencing lesson are detailed in Appendix
A.2, to keep this section focused on the architecture it justifies.
The finding that carries forward: none of those controls are claimed
by hardware sitting idle in a closet — they are claimed by the SD-WAN,
SASE, and diverse-transport architecture Section 4 already specifies,
which means the compliance case and the architecture case point at the
same build, not two different ones.

### 4.9 CISA telemetry continuity — CLAW and Protective DNS replace MTIPS

Regional breakout removes 1,500 branches from the MTIPS-provided
sensors that currently generate EINSTEIN 1 Enhanced (E1E) telemetry —
today's mechanism for sharing network visibility with CISA. That
telemetry does not survive the transition by default; it has to be
replaced, and CISA's own architecture guidance for exactly this
migration path names the replacement mechanism directly: agencies
moving from MTIPS to a SASE-based architecture route the equivalent
telemetry to CISA's Cloud Log Aggregation Warehouse
(CLAW).[^cisa-sase-tic3]

Two things about this belong in the program plan, not left implicit:

- **CLAW onboarding is a three-way coordination effort** — the agency,
  CISA, and the SD-WAN/SASE vendor — not a configuration change a
  network team completes alone. The guidance states this explicitly:
  implementing the integration "requires coordination among agencies,
  CISA, and [the SASE solution] to enable the secure and reliable
  transmission of relevant telemetry ... to CLAW."[^cisa-sase-tic3]
  That coordination has its own lead time, and it belongs on the
  Phase 0/1 critical path alongside the TIC 3.0 accreditation package
  Section 4.5 already names — not treated as a Phase 2 cutover detail
  discovered after circuits are already ordered.
- **MTIPS should not be decommissioned before CLAW telemetry is
  confirmed flowing.** Section 7's Phase 2 exit criterion should read
  as gated on confirmed CLAW parity, not on branch cutover completion
  alone: decommissioning MTIPS circuits before CISA confirms equivalent
  visibility through CLAW trades a compliance gap in E1E telemetry for
  a gap in transport — a worse position than the one being fixed, not
  a clean cutover.

The same integration point closes a second, independent federal
requirement. CISA's guidance directs agencies to route DNS traffic
through the SASE solution to CISA's Protective DNS service via DNS-
over-HTTPS — the mechanism CISA identifies as satisfying OMB M-22-09's
requirement to "resolve DNS queries using encrypted DNS wherever it is
technically supported."[^cisa-sase-tic3] This program's SD-WAN/SASE
build (Sections 4.4–4.5) is the natural place to configure that
integration; it should be scoped into Phase 1 alongside SSE enforcement
rather than deferred as a later enhancement.

CISA's own capability-to-technology mapping (Appendix A of the same
guidance) also cross-checks the control closures Appendix A.2 claims
for this program's architecture: CISA maps its TIC Policy Enforcement
Point (PEP) Security Capability Groups directly to SASE, NGFW, and IAM
— the same technology classes Section 4 already specifies — with DNS
PEP Capabilities mapped specifically to SASE plus Protective DNS, which
is the closure this subsection adds.[^cisa-sase-tic3]

[^cisa-sase-tic3]: [*The Journey to Zero Trust: Using Secure Access
    Service Edge in a Modern TIC 3.0 Solution*](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/using-sase-modern-tic-30-solution),
    CISA, June 2026, §5.5 (CISA Telemetry and Security Services) and
    Appendix A (TIC Security Capability Solutions, Table 2).

## 6. Cost Model and Sensitivity

### 6.1 Annual recurring cost at steady state

| Component | Basis | Annual |
|---|---|---|
| **Dedicated internet access, tiered by site class** | 750 at \$350, 525 at \$500, 225 at \$800 per month | \$8,460,000 |
| **5G secondary path** | 1,500 at \$75 per month | \$1,350,000 |
| **Cisco Networking Subscription, branch (Advantage)** | 1,500 at \$500 per year | \$750,000 |
| **Cisco Networking Subscription, hub** | 24 at \$3,000 per year | \$72,000 |
| **Analytics and control plane support** | Annual | \$100,000 |
| **Hub internet transit** | 12 at \$3,000 per month | \$432,000 |
| **Security service edge (SSE) licensing** | 70,000 users at \$65 per year | \$4,550,000 |
| **Total recurring** | — | **\$15,714,000** |
| **Less: MPLS retired** | 1,500 at \$1,200 per month | −\$21,600,000 |
| **Net annual position** | — | **−\$5,886,000** |

At steady state the program returns approximately \$5.9M per year
against the current transport baseline.

### 6.2 Five-year phased position

Savings ramp as branches migrate to local transport at MPLS contract
renewal, rather than arriving on day one.

| Year | Migration | Capital | Net savings | Cumulative |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | Design, hubs, pilot | \$10.0M | \$0 | −\$10.0M |
| **2** | 30% of branches | \$0 | \$1.77M | −\$8.23M |
| **3** | 70% of branches | \$0 | \$4.12M | −\$4.11M |
| **4** | 100% | \$0 | \$5.89M | +\$1.78M |
| **5** | Steady state | \$0 | \$5.89M | +\$7.67M |

**Comparison to the proposal:** the network program reaches a positive
cumulative cash position in year four. The distribution point refresh
reaches −\$50M in year one and recurs at the next refresh cycle. The
five-year delta between the two paths is approximately \$57.7M.

This comparison is not scope-for-scope, and that difference is
deliberate rather than an accounting convenience. The \$50M ask funds
content delivery only; the \$10M program funds the network
modernization that content delivery consolidation depends on, and that
same transport and hub investment also carries M365, Teams, TIC 3.0
breakout, and the Intune migration. Funding the hub and transport layer
once rather than paying for it piecemeal under separate initiatives is
the argument, not a bonus attached to it. A sponsor who wants the
content-delivery problem solved narrowly, with no interest in the other
workloads, should weigh the \$10.0M capital figure against the
transport-related recurring savings in Section 6.1 alone rather than
against the full capability list in the headline comparison.

### 6.3 Sensitivity to current MPLS cost

The entire financial case pivots on one number this paper does not
hold. The following table shows the outcome across plausible values.

| MPLS per site/month | Annual MPLS | Net annual position | Program character |
|---|---|---|---|
| **\$1,500** | \$27.0M | −\$11.29M | Strongly cash-positive |
| **\$1,200 (base case)** | \$21.6M | −\$5.89M | Cash-positive; self-funds in ~20 months |
| **\$873** | **\$15.7M** | **\$0** | **Breakeven** |
| **\$800** | \$14.4M | +\$1.31M | Modest net cost |
| **\$600** | \$10.8M | +\$4.91M | Net cost; justify on capability |
| **\$400** | \$7.2M | +\$8.51M | Net cost; the financial argument inverts |

::: {.callout-important}
## Breakeven threshold

The program breaks even at \$873 per site per month of current MPLS
spend.

Above that figure it funds itself and the recommendation is
unambiguous. Below it, the program remains architecturally correct and
remains cheaper than the \$50M proposal, but must be justified on
capability and mission grounds rather than on cost avoidance. Either
way it is a materially better use of funds than the distribution point
refresh — but the argument that persuades a budget authority differs,
and the paper should be revised accordingly once the number is known.
:::

## 7. Implementation Roadmap

| Phase | Timing | Activities | Exit criteria |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Phase 0** | Months 0–6 | Architecture and detailed design; TIC 3.0 Branch Office use case package and accreditation; on-premises SD-WAN control plane build; ten-site pilot spanning all transport types and tiers | Authority to operate for regional breakout; pilot sites stable for 30 days; validated per-site costs replacing the estimates in this paper |
| **Phase 1** | Months 6–18 | Twelve hub sites: SD-WAN aggregation, regional internet breakout, SSE enforcement, 24 consolidated distribution points, content library migration and prestaging; CLAW onboarding coordination initiated with CISA (Section 4.9) | All hubs in production; content served from hub tier; legacy field office DPs in read-only fallback; CLAW telemetry integration confirmed in the pilot sites |
| **Phase 2** | Months 18–48 | Branch migration in waves keyed to MPLS contract renewal dates: DIA and 5G installation, SD-WAN overlay, cutover, MPLS circuit termination | 100% of branches on local transport; MPLS decommissioned **only after CLAW telemetry parity is confirmed per branch** (Section 4.9); field office DPs retired |
| **Phase 3** | Months 36+ | Direct-breakout M365 optimization in production (DSCP-marked, application-aware routing per Section 4.6 — not INR); deploy Microsoft Connected Cache at hub sites as Intune workloads shift; retire distribution points as the Section 4.7 gates close, not on a fixed date | M365 path optimization in production within GCC's available mechanisms; MCC serving cloud-managed content; each Section 4.7 gate tracked and closed explicitly, with distribution points retired as they close |

### 7.1 Sequencing rationale

- **Accreditation, not procurement, is the critical path.** Circuits can
  be ordered in ninety days. A TIC 3.0 Branch Office authorization
  cannot. Phase 0 exists to remove that constraint before capital is
  committed at scale.
- **Hubs first, because they close three problems at once.** Phase 1
  delivers network aggregation, regional breakout, and the consolidated
  content tier in a single capital event at a single set of facilities
  under a single accreditation boundary.
- **Branch waves follow contract expiry, not geography.** Migrating at
  MPLS renewal avoids early termination liability and lets each wave
  fund the next.
- **Cloud dependencies are deferred to Phase 3, and INR is removed from
  scope entirely.** Nothing in Phases 0 through 2 depends on Connected
  Cache or co-management maturity, and — per Section 4.6 — Phase 3 does
  not depend on INR either, since GCC tenancy excludes it. If Connected
  Cache slips or fails accreditation, the program still delivers.
- **The all-in cutover is gated, not scheduled.** "Months 36+" in the
  Phase 3 row above is a placeholder, not a commitment. Section 4.7
  states the five conditions — app content, update content, OS
  provisioning, caching role, and compliance evidence — that actually
  determine when the last distribution point can be retired; track
  those, not the month number.

## 8. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk | Rating | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| **TIC 3.0 branch breakout accreditation slips** | High | Phase 0 begins with the accreditation package, not the design. Fall back to hub-only breakout, which is a defensible end state on its own and still eliminates the per-office DP requirement. A twelve-month slip pushes the year-4 breakeven in Section 6.2 to approximately year five; it does not change the five-year delta versus the \$50M refresh, since Phase 2 migration waves are keyed to MPLS contract renewal dates rather than a fixed calendar. |
| **Current MPLS cost is lower than assumed, inverting the financial case** | High | Validate before submission. If below breakeven, re-present the program on capability grounds; it remains cheaper than \$50M regardless. |
| **Crypto throughput licensed below circuit speed** | Medium | Specify throughput tier explicitly per platform in the bill of materials; validate under load during the Phase 0 pilot. |
| **Workstation-to-workstation SMB prohibited by segmentation policy** | Medium | Peer Cache is an optimization, not a dependency. If prohibited, branch content pulls directly from the hub tier over the new circuits, which are sized for it. |
| **Twelve hubs introduce new concentration risk** | Medium | HA pairs at every hub, diverse transport, and a defined branch fallback to a secondary hub in the SD-WAN policy. |
| **Terrestrial transport unavailable at some sites** | Medium | Serviceability survey in Phase 0. Historic rates suggest 5–15%; satellite or bonded cellular is appropriate for that subset only. |
| **Selected SSE vendor lacks FedRAMP Moderate authorization** | Medium | Confirm in Phase 0. Multiple SSE vendors hold FedRAMP Moderate authorization; the SD-WAN design is unaffected by the choice. |
| **Connected Cache unavailable or unsupported for GCC tenants** | Low | Confirm with the Microsoft account team. Nothing in Phases 0–2 depends on it; it affects only Phase 3 optimization. |
| **EIS task order modification across 1,500 sites delays transport** | Medium | Engage acquisition in Phase 0. Sequence Phase 2 waves to contract renewal dates already in the pipeline. |
| **CLAW onboarding lags branch cutover, leaving a telemetry gap when MTIPS is decommissioned** | High | Initiate the three-way CLAW coordination (agency, CISA, SASE/SD-WAN vendor) in Phase 0 alongside the accreditation package, not at Phase 2 cutover (Section 4.9). Gate each branch's MPLS decommission on confirmed CLAW telemetry parity for that site rather than on cutover completion alone. |
| **5G coverage inadequate at interior building locations** | Low | Per-site survey; outdoor-mount cellular gateway where interior signal is insufficient. |

## 9. Assumptions Requiring Validation

This paper is built on estimates. The following must be replaced with
agency data before any figure is used in a budget submission. They are
ordered by impact on the conclusion.

| # | Assumption | Value used | How to validate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Current MPLS cost per site per month | \$1,200 | Telecom contract records; determines whether the program is cash-positive |
| 2 | Managed endpoint population | 70,000 | Configuration Manager device count; drives distribution point count directly |
| 3 | Content library size | 1.5 TB | Measure SCCMContentLib on an existing distribution point |
| 4 | Seat distribution across 1,500 offices | 750 / 525 / 225 | Facilities and HR headcount by location |
| 5 | Terrestrial transport availability | 85–95% of sites | Serviceability survey against site addresses |
| 6 | Current TIC 3.0 posture | Not yet authorized for branch breakout | Confirm with the security architecture organization |
| 7 | Co-management maturity | Early | Track against the five gates in Section 4.7 (app content, update content, OS provisioning, caching role, compliance evidence) rather than estimating a calendar date; also paces the ADR-071 consolidation framing in Section 2.2 |
| 8 | Field office OS deployment requirement | Assumed centralized or vendor-staged | If offices re-image locally, revisit PXE and local content requirements |
| 9 | Workstation-to-workstation SMB permitted | Assumed prohibited | Network security policy; affects Peer Cache availability only |
| 10 | CLAW onboarding status and lead time | Not yet initiated | Confirm with the CISA Services Program (Section 4.9); determines whether Phase 0/1 timing needs to absorb three-way coordination lead time before any branch MPLS circuit can be decommissioned |

::: {.callout-note}
## Confidence statement

The architectural conclusion — that the content tier requires roughly
24 distribution points across 12 hub sites rather than 1,500 — is
derived from Microsoft published capacity limits and is robust across
the plausible range of assumptions 2 through 9.

The financial conclusion is not robust. It depends materially on
assumption 1. This paper should not be presented as a cost argument
until that number is confirmed.
:::

## 10. Recommendation

The proposed \$50,000,000 distribution point refresh solves content
delivery over constrained wide-area links at approximately 1,500 field
offices. It does so by distributing infrastructure rather than
correcting the underlying transport constraint, and it does so at a
moment when the agency has already committed to a management platform
that reduces the requirement.

A network modernization program addressing the same problem requires
approximately \$10.0M in first-year capital, reaches a positive
cumulative cash position in year four under base-case assumptions, and
delivers benefits across every cloud workload rather than one. It is
additionally a prerequisite for the Microsoft Intune migration already
underway, which means it is not a competing investment but an enabling
one.

### Recommended actions

1. Defer the \$50M distribution point refresh pending completion of a
   network modernization assessment.
2. Direct the sponsoring organization to state whether the \$50M figure
   is acquisition cost or five-year total cost of ownership, and to
   itemize any scope beyond the distribution point role.
3. Validate the nine assumptions in Section 9, beginning with current
   MPLS cost per site and managed endpoint population.
4. Fund Phase 0 — architecture, TIC 3.0 accreditation package, control
   plane build, and a ten-site pilot — at approximately \$1.8M over six
   months.
5. Confirm the planned distribution point count at completion of the
   co-management program, and the fiscal year in which it is reached.
   No refresh can be correctly sized without it.
6. Establish a single program governing network modernization and
   content tier consolidation, given that both resolve at the same
   twelve facilities.
7. Track the five gates in Section 4.7 — app content, update content,
   OS provisioning, caching role, and compliance evidence — as the
   explicit criterion for retiring the last distribution point, rather
   than defaulting to the Phase 3 calendar placeholder in Section 7.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Position statement for briefing

The \$50M distribution point refresh solves content delivery over
constrained field office links. An SD-WAN and regional breakout program
solves the same problem for roughly \$10M in capital, is expected to be
cash-positive by year four, is a prerequisite for the Intune migration
already underway, and delivers benefits to every other cloud workload.
Recommend deferring the distribution point refresh pending a network
modernization assessment.
:::

## Appendix A — Compliance and Reporting Detail

This appendix holds the control-by-control compliance detail referenced
from Sections 3.4 and 4.8. It is written for a security architecture or
ISSO audience; a reader focused on the budget and capacity case can
treat Sections 3.4 and 4.8's summary findings as sufficient and skip
this appendix entirely.

### A.1 Distribution points vs. Intune — a compliance comparison

Sections 3.1–3.3 make the economic and capacity case against the
per-office distribution point model. This section asks a different
question: independent of cost, how does a distribution point compare
to Intune on compliance grounds, and what does keeping any distribution
point tier alive cost in ongoing compliance work — on top of, not
instead of, whatever compliance program already covers the Intune-
managed endpoint fleet?

The two sit in structurally different compliance postures, not just
different maturity levels of the same one:

| Dimension | Configuration Manager distribution point | Intune |
|---|---|---|
| **Compliance boundary** | On-premises Windows Server + IIS site system role; the agency owns the entire customer-side stack | SaaS; the underlying service is covered by the Microsoft 365 GCC Moderate FedRAMP ATO, inherited by the agency through the standard FedRAMP customer responsibility matrix |
| **Hardening baseline** | DISA Windows Server STIG and IIS STIG apply and must be scanned independently, per server | Agency responsibility is limited to configuration (compliance policies, configuration profiles); the underlying service's own hardening is Microsoft's inherited CSP responsibility |
| **Vulnerability management (RA-5, SI-2)** | The agency runs vulnerability scanning and patch management against every distribution point's OS and IIS stack, indefinitely, for as many distribution points as exist | RA-5/SI-2 for the service backend is Microsoft's responsibility under the FedRAMP ATO; the agency's remaining SI-2 exposure is the endpoint OS layer, which is scanned regardless of whether a distribution point exists |
| **Continuous compliance evidence (CA-7)** | A distribution point has no compliance state of its own — successful content delivery is not a compliance claim, and a stalled or compromised distribution point is invisible to continuous monitoring unless separately instrumented | Native, continuous per-device compliance evaluation feeding Conditional Access in real time — the machine-verified evidence stream this corpus documents in [Ticket-to-Machine, Not Ticket-to-Human](ticket-to-machine-not-ticket-to-human.qmd) |
| **Transmission confidentiality (SC-8)** | Configurable — an HTTPS distribution point with a FIPS-validated certificate closes it — but this is a per-server configuration choice that must be verified, not a default | TLS to Microsoft's FedRAMP-authorized endpoints is standard by default |
| **System Security Plan footprint** | Every distribution point is its own system component: its own SSP entry, its own POA&M line items, its own place in the authorization boundary | Not a separate SSP component; already covered under the M365 GCC ATO boundary claimed for Intune-managed endpoints |

None of this is a substitution, and that is the point. For as long as
any distribution point exists — 1,500 today, 24 under this design's
Section 4 target, or whatever smaller number Section 4.7's gates
eventually allow — its STIG baseline, its vulnerability scan cadence,
and its SSP entry must be built and sustained as their own compliance
program, **in addition to**, not instead of, whatever compliance
program already covers the 70,000-endpoint Intune-managed fleet.
Section 6's cost model prices distribution point hardware and
licensing; it does not price this labor. Section 3.2's "compliance
sustainment" line item is this program, understated: consolidating to
24 distribution points shrinks it to roughly a twelfth of its former
size, but it does not shrink to zero, and it does not shrink at all
until Section 4.7's gates close.

### A.2 Compliance and reporting drivers, independent of cost

Sections 2 through 6 make the economic case: even under downside MPLS
assumptions, this program is cheaper than the proposed refresh. That
economic case is not the only one. NIST, CISA, and the OrgComp control-
closure ledger this corpus maintains give the agency reasons to build
SD-WAN and TIC 3.0 branch breakout at these 1,500 sites that hold even
if Section 6.3's sensitivity analysis had come out unfavorably.

**NIST SP 800-53 controls a flat MPLS branch with centralized-only
inspection leaves unclaimed or weakly claimed.** The full mapping —
control by control, with the evidence source for each — is maintained
in [SD-WAN vs. DIA Under TIC 3.0](tic3-sdwan-vs-dia.qmd), §5, and in
Vol I Book 07 of the Federal Organization Compliance series; this
section states only which of those closures land at field offices
specifically, not the derivation:

- **SC-7 (Boundary Protection) and SC-7(4)** — a governed distributed
  policy enforcement point at the regional hub, not the flat branch
  circuit itself, is what makes local egress an assessed boundary
  rather than a gap in one.
- **SC-8 / SC-8(1) (Transmission Confidentiality, Cryptographic
  Protection)** — closed by the SD-WAN overlay's circuit-wide IPsec,
  not by the DIA/MPLS pipe underneath it.
- **AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement) and SI-3 (Malicious Code
  Protection)** — provided by the SASE/SSE stack this program's Phase 1
  deploys at the hub tier (Section 4.5), not by the branch router.
- **SI-4 and AU-12 (System Monitoring, Audit Generation)** — the
  application-aware routing and path telemetry this program's SD-WAN
  overlay generates is the evidence source; a static branch circuit
  generates none of it.
- **CP-8 (Telecommunications Services), CP-8(2) and CP-8(3) (Single
  Points of Failure, Provider Diversity)** — closed directly by this
  program's own dual-path branch design in Section 4.4: DIA plus a
  physically diverse 5G secondary path at all 1,500 sites is the
  CP-8(2)/CP-8(3) closure, not an add-on to it.

None of these controls are claimed by hardware sitting idle in a
closet. They are claimed by the SD-WAN, SASE, and diverse-transport
architecture this paper's Section 4 already specifies — which means
the compliance case and the architecture case point at the same build,
not two different ones.

**CISA's Zero Trust Maturity Model v2.0 cross-cutting capabilities**
— Visibility and Analytics, Automation and Orchestration, and
Governance — run underneath every pillar, not beside them, per
[Zero Trust Governance Principles](zero-trust-governance-principles.qmd).
A flat MPLS branch fleet is opaque to all three: there is no correlated
telemetry to see, no policy surface to automate against, and nothing
for governance to enforce. Twelve governed hub sites with SD-WAN and
SASE telemetry are what give the Network pillar a cross-cutting
capability to report at all — this is a maturity-model argument, not
only a security one, and it applies whether or not the MPLS economics
in Section 6.3 favor the program.

**BOD-25-01's discipline applies here even though its text does not.**
CISA [Binding Operational Directive 25-01](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/bod-25-01-implementing-secure-practices-cloud-services)
governs Microsoft 365 tenant configuration, not branch network
architecture — it is not itself a network mandate, and this paper does
not claim otherwise. What transfers is the sequencing lesson
[Assessment Tools vs. Closing BOD-25-01 Findings](bod-25-01-close-before-assess.qmd)
documents for M365 baselines: an assessment tool that measures
deviation from a control is not the same claim as having closed it.
Running a ZTMM self-assessment or a network vulnerability scan against
1,500 flat, ungoverned branch egress points produces the same growing
deviation list that paper describes for unremediated SCuBA findings —
the assessment keeps finding the gap; only the SD-WAN/SASE build in
Section 4 closes it. Remediate first, then assess, applies to the
network layer exactly as it applies to the tenant layer.
